question: What is the main goal of the Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) model in public hospitals?

options.A: To replace state government health budgets entirely
options.B: To fund free housing for incoming medical staff
options.C: To ensure a steady supply of essential medicines
options.D: To generate heavy profit for hospital management

explanation: You've got this! The DRF uses money from drug sales strictly to restock those same drugs, keeping our pharmacy shelves stocked so we never run out unexpectedly. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why can a strict cash-and-carry drug policy cause ethical worries in public hospitals?

options.A: It lowers the overall quality of manufactured pharmaceutical drugs
options.B: It makes basic medicines too expensive for the hospital to buy
options.C: It forces nurses to spend too much time counting inventory
options.D: It can block poor and vulnerable patients from getting lifesaving care

explanation: Spot on! When payment is required upfront before dispensing, patients who lack cash might be denied the critical treatment they urgently need. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of DRF exemptions in healthcare facilities?

options.A: To punish patients who refuse to pay hospital bills
options.B: To increase the daily revenue of the drug fund
options.C: To provide a financial safety net for vulnerable patients
options.D: To help the hospital pharmacy clear out expired drugs

explanation: Think of exemptions as a safety cushion designed to protect patients who truly cannot afford the cost of their medications. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h2)

question: How do DRF exemptions help protect public health in the wider community?

options.A: By ensuring contagious diseases are treated promptly without financial delay
options.B: By providing government grants to local chemical manufacturing plants
options.C: By lowering the market price of medical equipment for private clinics
options.D: By forcing pharmaceutical companies to lower their manufacturing costs

explanation: Great thinking! Treating infectious illnesses right away stops the disease from spreading further among the general public. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which group is usually eligible for DRF exemptions in our hospitals?
explanation: Older adults who lack pensions or family financial backup are standard beneficiaries of these hospital welfare safety nets. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h3)

question: Why is having clear rules for DRF exemptions so important for hospital staff?

options.A: It stops staff from showing personal bias when giving out free drugs
options.B: It allows the pharmacy to increase drug prices for wealthy patients
options.C: It ensures that doctors do not have to write any medical prescriptions
options.D: It guarantees that the federal government will pay the hospital bonus funds

explanation: Clear criteria remove guesswork and favoritism, making sure that only genuinely qualified patients receive free medications. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h3)

question: What type of care usually triggers automatic DRF exemptions during an emergency?
explanation: When every second counts, emergency trauma care gets fast-tracked so lifesaving supplies are never delayed by paperwork. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h4)

question: A child is rushed to the ward with severe, complicated malaria. What is the best first step regarding their medications?

options.A: Refuse treatment until the family pays cash for the full prescription
options.B: Wait for hospital accountants to review the family's bank statements
options.C: Send the parents out to buy drugs from a commercial chemist across the street
options.D: Provide necessary emergency anti-malarials immediately under the exemption policy

explanation: Spot on! Severe pediatric emergencies qualify for immediate medication access to save the child's life without delay. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h4)

question: What happens to a drug revolving fund over time if free drugs are given out but never paid for by a subsidy?

options.A: The pharmacy inventory will steadily deplete and collapse
options.B: The government will automatically double its funding
options.C: The fund will grow larger and more profitable
options.D: Drug manufacturers will begin supplying free items forever

explanation: Remember, a revolving fund depends on money returning when drugs are sold. If stock is given away without a replacement fund, the pharmacy will soon run out of cash to restock. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h5)

question: Where should the money come from to pay for drugs given out under an exemption policy?

options.A: Extra fees charged secretly to other ordinary patients
options.B: Deductions taken directly from the personal salaries of nurses
options.C: Dedicated external subsidy pools, grants, or hospital subventions
options.D: Donations collected from patients waiting in the outpatient queue

explanation: External funds or hospital subventions must reimburse the DRF account so that providing free care to the poor doesn't ruin the pharmacy stock. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which hospital department usually conducts the financial check for an exemption request?
explanation: Social workers are specially trained to assess a patient's financial background and verify hardship before approving welfare waivers. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h6)

question: Why is a formal approval process necessary before giving out free drugs from the DRF?

options.A: To make sure patients wait a very long time in the hall
options.B: To give the pharmacy staff extra paperwork to complete daily
options.C: To prevent fraud and ensure the fund remains sustainable
options.D: To discourage sick people from coming to the public hospital

explanation: Proper documentation protects the revolving fund from being drained by unauthorized requests, keeping it alive for those who truly need it. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge facing DRF exemptions in public hospitals?

options.A: Persistent stockouts caused by lack of reimbursement
options.C: Exploitation of loopholes by non-indigent individuals
options.D: Excessive government funding that overflows the pharmacy

explanation: If only! Public hospitals rarely have excessive funding; instead, they constantly battle underfunding and delayed subventions. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h7)

question: How do communication breakdowns between hospital departments affect the DRF exemption process?

options.A: They force the federal government to send more medical equipment
options.B: They cause delays in patient care and lead to lost exemption vouchers
options.C: They automatically increase the overall monthly revenue of the pharmacy
options.D: They improve the working relationship between doctors and pharmacists

explanation: When departments fail to communicate well, vulnerable patients suffer dangerous delays while waiting for their paperwork to clear. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why are nurses in a great position to spot patients who need DRF exemptions?

options.A: They make the final legal decisions on hospital budgets
options.B: They personally purchase all the drugs sold in the pharmacy
options.C: They are responsible for auditing the hospital's bank accounts
options.D: They spend the most direct time at the patient's bedside

explanation: Because nurses are constantly at the bedside, they are the first to notice when a patient is struggling to afford their prescribed medications. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h8)

question: A nurse discovers that a struggling patient in the ward cannot buy their prescribed antibiotics. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Advocate for the patient by contacting the social welfare unit for an exemption
options.B: Reprimand the patient for coming to the hospital without money
options.C: Ignore the situation because financial matters are outside nursing duties
options.D: Discharge the patient immediately from the hospital ward

explanation: You nailed it! As patient advocates, nurses bridge the gap by connecting vulnerable patients with social welfare so they can get their meds without delay. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h8)
